sections.heading: Seeing that I have nothing to boast about
sections.text:
Lord, you are holy enough to humble me and gentle enough to let me come near. Please do not let pride grow in my heart.

I am made from the dust, and one day my body will return to it. Anything that seems impressive in me—my mind, my abilities, my health, my personality, my opportunities—is not something I created or earned. It is all your gift. If I have more than someone else in any way, it is because you have been kind, not because I have made myself great.
theological_themes: Human life is created, dependent, and mortal.
Every natural ability is an undeserved gift from God, leaving no room for boasting.

scripture_references.connection: This passage grounds the prayer’s reminder that human beings are dust and return to dust. It cuts against pride by placing human strength and beauty under the reality of creaturely mortality.
Paul directly challenges boasting by asking what anyone has that was not received. That supports the prayer’s confession that every faculty and advantage is a gift, not a personal ground for pride.

sections.heading: Seeing my sin honestly before you
sections.text:
And as small as I am as a creature, I am lower still as a sinner. I have broken your law again and again. Sin has marked me more deeply than I like to admit. It has bent my desires, darkened my thoughts, and touched what I do with corruption.

So how can I parade myself as if I were something great? Before you, I have no reason to lift myself up. Show me myself as you see me, because when I see the truth, pride cannot survive.
theological_themes: Sin is not merely weakness but guilt before God’s law.
True self-knowledge comes from seeing oneself in God’s sight.
Pride withers when sin is honestly confessed before God.

scripture_references.connection: Paul shows that God’s law silences human boasting because all are guilty before God and fall short of his glory. This directly supports the prayer’s movement from creaturely lowliness to deeper moral humbling as a sinner.
David’s confession treats sin as something personally known and deeply rooted, not superficial. It gives biblical language for the prayer’s honest admission that sin has marked the whole person.

sections.heading: Asking you to make me low enough to receive grace
sections.text:
Humble me before you, Lord, and then fill my empty hands with the good things only you can give.

Water does not stay on the bare tops of hills; it runs down and brings life to the low places. Make me willing to be low before you—not pretending, not self-hating, but truly humbled—so that your grace can settle in me and bear fruit.
theological_themes: God gives grace to the humble, not to the self-exalting.
Humility is not despair but the right posture for receiving spiritual blessing.
God’s gifts produce fruit in those who know their need.

scripture_references.connection: James contrasts pride with humility before God and calls believers to humble themselves under his hand. The passage supports the prayer’s request to be made low so that grace, not self-importance, fills the heart.
God is exalted and holy, yet he dwells with the contrite and lowly to revive them. This illuminates the image of spiritual life flowing into the low places.

sections.heading: Let my failures make me more watchful, not more proud
sections.text:
When I leave undone what you have called me to do, let that conviction strip pride away from me. Do not let me excuse myself or compare myself into comfort. Use even the sting of a guilty conscience to pull me back into devotion to your service.

Make me more careful, more awake, and more ready to obey you in the ordinary duties I would rather neglect.
theological_themes: Neglected obedience exposes pride and spiritual carelessness.
Godly conviction should lead to renewed devotion, not despair or self-justification.
Faithfulness includes watchfulness in ordinary duties.

scripture_references.connection: James names the guilt of knowing the good one ought to do and failing to do it. This supports the prayer’s concern not only with active rebellion but also with neglected duties.
Paul calls believers to walk carefully and understand the Lord’s will. That fits the prayer’s request for more watchful care in daily obedience.

sections.heading: Holding on to Christ when pride and temptation come
sections.text:
When I start thinking too highly of myself, open my eyes to the cunning power of my spiritual enemy. Keep me alert. Help me stand by faith, watching carefully, not trusting my own strength.

Teach me to cling tightly to Jesus, my humble Lord. If I fall, let me run to him and hide in the righteousness that is mine only in my Redeemer. And when you keep me from falling, do not let me take credit for that either. Let me say plainly: all my rescue, all my endurance, and all my deliverance come from your grace.

Keep me humble. Keep me gentle. Keep me low before you.
theological_themes: Pride is spiritually dangerous and leaves a person vulnerable to temptation.
The believer’s safety is found in watchful faith and dependence on Christ.
When believers fall, their refuge is Christ’s righteousness, not their own performance.
Deliverance from temptation is by God’s grace, not self-sufficiency.

scripture_references.connection: Peter connects humility before God with alertness against the devil, who seeks to devour. This strongly supports the prayer’s link between pride, spiritual danger, and watchful faith.
Christ’s humility is the pattern and anchor for the believer’s humility. The prayer’s phrase “my humble Lord” is grounded in the Son of God humbling himself in obedience.
Paul rejects any righteousness of his own and seeks the righteousness from God through faith in Christ. This supports the prayer’s desire to hide in the Redeemer’s righteousness after falling.
Paul teaches that God provides a way of escape in temptation. That grounds the prayer’s confession that any escape or deliverance must be credited to God’s grace.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original uses very severe language about human lowliness, including comparison to reptiles and being “less than nothing” before God. I preserved the humbling force while avoiding wording that could imply human beings lack value as God’s image-bearers.
The prayer strongly connects conviction of neglected duty with spiritual growth. I rendered this as godly conviction leading to renewed devotion, not as morbid self-condemnation or despair.
significant_interpretive_choices: I interpreted “O Thou Terrible Meek” as addressing God in his holy majesty and gentle condescension, rather than trying to reproduce the paradoxical phrase directly.
I kept the original image of water flowing down from barren heights to fertile low places, because it carries the prayer’s central picture of humility as the place where grace bears fruit.
I rendered “hide myself in my Redeemer’s righteousness” in explicitly Christ-centered terms, connecting it to justification by faith rather than general moral improvement.
